checks.detail: Every figure here was measured by THIS builder on 2026-07-26 with its command and revision, except figures explicitly attributed to a reviewer. THE ROUND-4 SENTENCE `Three classes do' IS CORRECTED: at round 4 FOUR classes could defeat the stage - the bash-startup class, PATH, PYTHONPATH, and the git-variable class the review found - and after this round the environment reaching the interpreter is exactly PATH, so what remains is the bash-startup class and PATH itself, with the git class and PYTHONPATH closed and PYTHONHOME never having belonged. Every count in this manifest is derived from a stated command, which is the fix for the class of slip the last three reviews each caught once. THE ONE CLAIM THIS MANIFEST DELIBERATELY DOES NOT MAKE: that the text guard is complete. It is not, and the four routes that defeat it are declared below.

assumptions: ROUND 5 EXISTS FOR ONE FALSE SENTENCE THIS ITEM NEWLY WROTE, and the lesson is the one it has now been taught four times in different clothes. Round 4 pinned the argv SHAPE of every subprocess call and concluded from that the stage could not shell out to something that reads the environment. The conclusion does not follow: a whitelisted command can itself be an environment reader, and `git` is a spectacular one. The rule that keeps holding is that a guard keyed on the ROUTES someone thought of is blind to the rest, and the closure has to be over the DOMAIN - here the environment crossing a process boundary, closed by passing one variable by name instead of by removing the hostile ones.

WHAT THE TEXT GUARD DOES NOT CLOSE, DECLARED BECAUSE THE ROUND-4 REVIEW MEASURED IT AND BECAUSE STRENGTHENING IT IS EXPLICITLY ANOTHER ITEM'S WORK. Four routes defeat the guard's four rules, two of them carrying a GREEN gate at 3200 / 0. The serious one is ALIASING: `_r = subprocess.run` then `_r([...])`, because the argv rule inspects only Calls whose func is an Attribute on the Name `subprocess`, so an alias sits outside rule 4 entirely - and an alias is an ORDINARY REFACTOR, not an obfuscation. The others are split-literal spellings (`open("/proc/self/envi" "ron")`, `vars(subprocess)["o" "s"]`, `sys.modules["o" "s"]`, where the unsplit forms ARE caught) and free ARGUMENT CONTENT, since the shape is the tuple of string constants only. Closing this properly needs AST alias tracking, which is real engineering rather than a patch, and it was NOT attempted here on instruction. RECORDED FOR THAT ITEM: `["git", "ls-files", _NARROW]` gives `lint: pass (0 python, 0 shell)` and is caught only by the file-set-equality assertions, not by the guard. NOTE WHAT THE BOUNDARY DOES FOR ALL OF THESE: an aliased or split-literal environment read now finds an environment holding only PATH, so the guard's gap costs less than it did before this round, which is why the boundary was the right thing to build first.

(1) BASH_ENV names a file bash sources before line 1 of this script, measured by the round-4 reviewer as a false pass, and nothing inside the file can close it; the same holds for anything acting on bash while it reads the file. PATH is conceded, round 2. (2) The guard is over the stage's TEXT, so it catches an EDIT and not a hostile interpreter. (3) A failure that kills the process outright is named by nothing; the round-2 reviewer verified this declared limit TRUE and failing closed on all four forced deaths. (5) Round-1 note N4 stands unfixed and out of scope: neither stage handles a tracked path containing a space, faithfully preserved bug for bug, and no such path is tracked.
